extracted.intended_audience: general public, students, researchers, and policymakers interested in military/information operations
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic overview of information warfare covering definitions, techniques, examples, doctrines, and legal/ethical concerns. Suitable as a reference summary of forms, actors, and practical issues in state and non-state information operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Information warfare (IW) is the battlespace use and management of information and communication technology (ICT) in pursuit of a competitive advantage over an opponent. It is the manipulation of information trusted by a target without the target's awareness so that the target will make decisions against their interest but in the interest of the one conducting information warfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article emphasizes both the technological (ICT) and cognitive (manipulation of trusted information) aspects; it also notes ambiguity about timing and severity: 'As a result, it is not clear when information warfare begins, ends, and how strong or destructive it is.' Use this definition to identify operations that combine ICT means with covert manipulation of belief/decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction from cyberwarfare
rubrics_metrics.description: Information warfare is different from cyberwarfare that attacks computers, software, and command control systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat cyberwarfare as operations that directly target computer systems and networks; treat information warfare as broader efforts that may use ICT to manipulate perceptions, deny information, or shape decisions even when not directly damaging software/hardware.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary objectives / operational functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Information warfare may involve the collection of tactical information; assurance(s) that one's information is valid; spreading of propaganda or disinformation to demoralize or manipulate the enemy and the public; undermining the quality of the opposing force's information; and denial of information-collection opportunities to opposing forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These five functions (collection, assurance, influence via propaganda/disinformation, degradation of enemy information quality, denial of enemy intelligence collection) form a practical checklist for evaluating whether an activity qualifies as information warfare and what objective it serves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques and tactical methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques include jamming television, internet and radio transmissions; hijacking channels for disinformation campaigns; disabling logistics networks; disabling or spoofing enemy communications networks (including online social communities); sabotaging stock exchange transactions by electronic intervention, leaking sensitive information or placing disinformation; and using drones and other surveillance robots or webcams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing an operation, look for one or more of these concrete methods. Examples from the article (Gulf War, Moonlight Maze) illustrate real-world application. Methods overlap with electronic warfare, cyber operations, and physical logistics/sabotage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of social media and synthetic media
rubrics_metrics.description: The organized use of social media and other online content-generation platforms can be used to influence public perceptions; synthetic media is listed as a communication management tool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate campaigns for coordinated account networks, influencer promotion, hashtag manipulation, creation/use of deepfakes or other synthetic content, and search-result manipulation (e.g., pushing alternate narratives into Google News). The article cites state efforts to promote influencers and use hashtags as illustrative tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational advantages of non-kinetic methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Disabling communications networks electronically provides a safer alternative to kinetic attacks, allows rapid re-enablement after occupation, and can yield tactical benefits (e.g., eavesdropping, cutting off communications at critical moments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion highlights why military planners may prefer electronic or information-based interdiction: lower risk to personnel and reversible effects. Use it to weigh strategic benefits versus potential legal/ethical costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution and non-attribution challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-attribution is a fundamental challenge: online identity may not serve as proof of real-world identity, making it hard to confirm state responsibility for cyber/information attacks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating incidents, treat attribution as probabilistic; lack of technical proof complicates political and legal responses. Assessments should account for plausible deniability and covert tradecraft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and ethical concerns about risk asymmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Information warfare raises moral and legal ambiguities because the risk for the initiating party is substantially lower than for traditional attack, which makes it easier for governments, terrorist or criminal organizations to conduct attacks more frequently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this criterion to evaluate the proportionality and likely frequency of operations; it underpins calls for updated norms, law, and policy to deter abuse and manage escalation risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civilian-technology targeting and privacy implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Because ICTs are deeply integrated into civilian life, civilian technologies and infrastructures can be targeted, and attacks may be launched through civilian computers or websites; this complicates enforcement and raises privacy concerns and ethical issues about targeting civilians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess operations for civilian harm, collateral effects, and privacy violations. Policies and doctrinal guidance (see Lt. Gen. Alexander quote) urge limiting impact on civilians and considering privacy rights when planning operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability difficulties for automated and cyber systems
rubrics_metrics.description: The mass-integration of ICT and the use of robotic/automated systems make it increasingly hard to determine who is responsible for particular events, an issue exacerbated in cyberattacks where tracing initiators can be virtually impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging incidents or crafting doctrine, explicitly consider attribution limits, command responsibility, and legal frameworks for autonomous/automated actions to avoid accountability gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: State doctrine and institutionalization
rubrics_metrics.description: NATO defines information war as 'an operation conducted in order to gain an information advantage over the opponent.' The U.S. Air Force has had Information Warfare Squadrons since the 1980s and the U.S. DoD publishes doctrine (Information Operations Roadmap, JP 3-13 series, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use published doctrines and organizational structures as benchmarks for what states consider legitimate IW tasks and acceptable tactics. Presence of doctrine and units indicates institutionalization and standard operating approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical indicators and notable examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Notable examples include Chinese 'informatized warfare' (battlefield management systems, precision-strike capabilities, C4ISR and state propaganda/influence operations), Russian interference in foreign elections and disinformation campaigns (e.g., 2016 US elections, 2024 activity), and U.S. campaigns (e.g., alleged COVID-19 disinformation efforts). The article also cites manipulation of search results and promotion of influencers as indicators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these empirical patterns as signals when diagnosing information warfare: coordinated disinformation, search-result manipulation, influencer promotion, state-aligned messaging, and cross-platform amplification. Examples help map tactics to strategic aims and to evaluate attribution likelihood and impact.
